linkedin.about:
Brené Brown is a research professor at the University of Houston, where she holds the Huffington Foundation Endowed Chair at the Graduate College of Social Work. She also holds the position of Professor of Practice in Management at The University of Texas at Austin McCombs School of Business.

Brené is the author of six #1 New York Times bestsellers and the host of two award-winning podcasts. Brené spends most of her time working in organizations around the world, helping develop braver leaders and more courageous cultures. In 2024, she was named Executive Chair of the Center for Daring Leadership at BetterUp. She lives in Houston, Texas, with her husband, Steve. They have two children, Ellen and Charlie, and a weird Bichon Frisé named Lucy.

When we see people attack empathy or say things like, “The fundamental weakness of Western civilization is empathy” (Elon Musk, 2025), we should ask ourselves, “What harm, pain, or hurt do they not want us to see or feel? Who do they want to hurt, humiliate, or dehumanize without accountability?”

Based on our research over the past 25 years, creating meaningful connections and human-centered systems requires a combination of compassion and cognitive empathy. I think of compassion as the daily practice and cognitive empathy as one its most powerful tools.

We define compassion as the daily practice of recognizing and accepting our shared humanity so that we treat ourselves and others with loving-kindness, and we take action in the face of suffering.

Most definitions of compassion share a commitment to action. It’s not just feeling, it’s doing. Compassion is fueled by accepting that we’re all made of strength and struggle—no one is immune to pain or suffering. Compassion is not a practice of “better than” or “I can fix you”—it’s a practice based in the beauty and pain of shared humanity.

Most researchers agree there are at least two elements to empathy: cognitive empathy and affective empathy. Cognitive empathy, sometimes called perspective taking, is the ability to recognize and understand another person’s emotions. Affective empathy, often called experience sharing, is one’s own emotional attunement with another person’s experience.

The empathy we desperately need is understanding what someone is feeling, not feeling it for them. If someone feels lonely, empathy doesn’t require us to feel lonely too, only to reach back into our own experience with loneliness so we can understand and connect. Affective empathy, feeling something along with the person who is struggling, is a slippery slope toward becoming too overwhelmed to offer meaningful support.

Again, empathy is a tool of compassion. We can respond empathically only if we are willing to be present to someone’s pain. If we’re not willing to do that, it’s not real empathy. And the lack of real empathy is 100% a major threat to civilizations.

Thank you to @toninovvva for this powerful reminder.

This is one of my favorite @thecuriosityshop episodes. In a world where everyone and everything is fighting for our attention, our rage, and our money, we exam what makes us vulnerable to persuasion and how we can develop stronger influence literacy skills. 

It’s the best kind of collision between Adam’s, “think like a scientist” research and my work on shame and vulnerability. 

Biggest finding: 
Shame around being persuadable makes us more vulnerable to influence. Acknowledging that we are vulnerable to those reels and TikTok’s and snake oil pitches makes us more resistant! 

If you want to dive into the original research - all of the studies are cited in the show notes for the podcast. 

You can download or watch the episode now!

@adamgrant and I loved talking with @angelalduckworth about her new book, “Situated.”

Big takeaway:

“To stay motivated through the countless hours of practice that separate amateurs from experts, grit is necessary but not sufficient. The situation also matters—and to an astonishing degree:

Culture matters.
Mentors matter.
Teammates matter.
Even the objects in your personal space matter.

How you think about your goals and what you’re willing to do to achieve them depends on both you and your situation.”

I also loved our conversation about billboards - those signs we post around our spaces as reminders of what’s important. It reminds of why I like to write in a room where my children’s art is hanging. The kids’ art is my favorite art and it’s imperfect and honest. Grit is great, but I also need the environment to say, “Have fun. Just start.”

To watch or listen to the episode, head to YouTube or wherever you listen to podcasts.

Priya Parker, one of my favorite thinkers and writers, is joining @thecuriosityshop this week and we’re talking about fighting! Not “dukes up” fighting but how real heat and conflict can build connection if we’re willing to learn how to do it well.

What I love about this conversation and Priya’s new book - “The Art of Fighting” - is being called to imagine a world where we unlearn and relearn what it means to gather and to disagree. And, she’s just so honest and fun!

To watch or listen to the full episode, head to YouTube or wherever you listen to podcasts.

Aaron Sandel @prof.sandel, an anthropologist and primatologist, has spent over a decade studying the Ngogo chimpanzees, witnessing one of the largest known chimp communities split into two factions.

Aaron helps Adam and I understand what chimpanzees can teach us about friendship, conflict, belonging, and human nature. He shares what he learned from watching these chimps show affection, navigate dominance hierarchies, and face the effects of division within their own community.

Aaron also reflects on what it was like to watch chimps he knew by name turn against one another, while exploring the surprising depth of bonds in this community.

If you’re trying to find me this semester, I’ll be the one sneaking into Aaron’s class at UT Austin! I have so many more questions!

To listen or watch the full episode, head to YouTube or wherever you listen to podcasts.

Grateful for a mother who warned her daughters about the price she paid for trying to conform to nice girl culture in the 1950’s. We didn’t know all of the details of her wounds, but we fully understood the depth of her pain. 

When she died she had framed pictures of Gloria Steinem and Angela Davis over her desk.

Celebrating Dolly has me thinking about the joy of reading books and how often I squander that pleasure by putting myself under pressure to consume pages. 

We are all craving deep reading, deep thinking, and deep connection — and these all require deep time. 

I went back this morning and re-read the interview we did with @mayasmarty and was drawn to her phrase the “privilege of focus.” 

Let’s start a spiritual book club where we read what we want, when we want, no meetings or deadlines - just a shared reframe of deep time as subversive in a world of shallow distraction, addictive scrolling, and unrelenting attention grabbing. ❤️📖❤️

Sometimes shiny is great. Sometimes it’s dangerous.

Episode available on YouTube or wherever you listen to podcasts.
